title: The Long Way Home
summary: The Guild has served Old Bahro an eviction notice for forty years of sitting on a crate he insists is a footrest. His legal strategy is simple and ancient: the notice must be delivered to the wrong dock, returned with apologies, and served again next season. Ride the paper on its traditional long way home.

objectives.label: Accept the earnest brown envelope from Old Bahro
Deliver it to the wrong dock — Keel Town, Hang-Tenant Services
Return it to the Guild exchange, stamped UNDELIVERABLE, with the Guild's compliments

offer.text: Young'un. The Guild has served me a paper. It says my crate is an unlawful dwellment, my mast is encroached, and my person is to vacate. Forty-first time they've sent it. I treasure the series; I have opinions on the binding.

Now. Longstanding arrangement. You take the paper, you ride it all the way out to Keel Town — the wrong dock, very wrong, beautifully wrong — where a clerk of my acquaintance stamps it UNDELIVERABLE and writes something kind in the margin. Then you walk it back to the exchange with apologies. By the time the Guild re-serves it, soup season. Every year. Like weather.

Is it legal? The paper has survived six audits, two acting factors, and a fire I am legally required to describe as adjacent. At this point the Guild doesn't want me gone, young'un. The notice *is* the tenancy. Evicting me would bankrupt the form.

accept.text: Envelope's earnest and brown, stamped FIRST and FINAL for the fortieth time. Mind you deliver it wrong properly — Hang-Tenant Services, window three, ask for Dessa, tell her the mast still creaks in E-flat. She'll know the paper.
So to be clear: I'm being paid to misdeliver government mail, on retainer, annually.
You're being paid to preserve a tradition older than the road that built it. The misdelivery is merely folk customs. Over.

complete.text: Delivered wrong, stamped, margin-noted, and walked home to the exchange. Dessa says hello. The exchange clerk sighed in a way I can only describe as *heritage*.

Forty-one for forty-one, then. The Guild gets its motion, clerk Dessa gets her hello, I get my mast, and you, young'un, get paid in honest credits and honorary soup. The system's perfect. Nobody touch it.

Courier. Whatever the old man's envelope says, the Guild's official position is that it was handled with *uncharacteristic* thoroughness. We've billed the round trip to an account called TRADITIONAL MAINTENANCE. Do not ask me whose tradition. The account predates me.
